newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish forestry views steady after Swedes report.
newsitem.headline: Finnish forestry views steady after Swedes report.

text.p: Significant falls in Swedish forestry firms' profits in 1996 are in line with expectations and spell no change in forecasts or recommendations for their Finnish rivals, analysts said on Thursday.

Swedish SCA's and Stora's 38 percent and 71 percent falls in respective profits and comments on Wednesday and Thursday confirmed the industry's near-term woes but brought little news about the expected upturn, they said.
Aktia Bank forestry analyst Paivi Palomaki said Stora was the first forest industry firm to spell out that the upturn analysts are waiting for would be coming this year.
"I don't think this was negative, rather the opposite," she said. "Stora was the first to say that an upturn is coming."
She referred particularly to the management's comments at a telephone briefing to analysts.
Palomaki said Aktia has a general buy recommendation on forestry stocks and said there was no reason to change this.
But Merita Bank's Anna-Maija Pirskanen said SCA's statement -- that the price trend in pulp was down rather than up -- was confusing in the context of expected price hikes in fine paper.
"Some with a positive view may go more negative on this," she said, adding Merita's rating on forestries was underweight.
The Finnish forestry companies are due to release 1996 profits starting on February 10 with Metsa-Serla. UPM-Kymmene's and Enso's reports are due a month later, on March 4 and March 10 respectively.

Arctos analyst Jukka Huuskonen said the Finnish companies may have had a relatively better final part of the year than the Swedes, who suffered from the crown's relative strengthening on top of subdued forest industry product markets.
SCA said 13 percent of its 38 percent fall in 1996 profits was attributable to the stronger crown.
Stora's 1996 net income fell to 1.56 billion crowns from 5.37 billion in 1995 and it said 750 million of this was due to the stronger currency.
The Finnish forest industry companies reported their highest ever profits in 1995, but earnings plunged already in the first four months of 1996.
Metsa-Serla's 1995 profit after financial items was 1.91 billion markka and Enso's was 3.52 billion markka.
Kymmene and Repola, which merged in 1996 to form UPM-Kymmene, posted a 6.3 billion markka joint 1995 profit.

In January-August, UPM-Kymmene's profit fell to 2.67 billion from 4.54 billion in the same period in 1995, Enso's profit fell to 1.16 billion from 2.68 billion and Metsa-Serla's fell to 254 million from 1.29 billion.
